Sample text:
---
The first thing I repaired for money was a clock that had nothing wrong with it. I was twelve. Mrs. Alvarez brought it across the landing wrapped in a dish towel, though it was an ordinary plastic kitchen clock with a picture of a rooster on its face. She said it lost ten minutes every morning. I put it on my desk, watched it through lunch, and reported that it kept excellent time. She gave me two dollars anyway. Years later I learned that her husband had been turning it back so she would sit with him a little longer over coffee.

My father repaired shoes in a narrow shop below our apartment. He disliked the word *cobbler*, which customers used with an air of having remembered the name of a rare bird. “Shoe repair is fine,” he would say. He let me keep a drawer under the counter for the small appliances people brought after Mrs. Alvarez recommended me. Most needed batteries. One radio needed its volume knob pushed firmly back onto the stem. My father watched me return it to a delighted cabdriver and said, “You know, there are jobs where they pay you even when you don’t get lucky.”

The shop smelled of leather, rubber, and the orange my father peeled at three each afternoon. He took the skin off in one piece and laid it on the radiator in winter. He could recognize certain customers by the sound of their approach. There was a school principal who landed hard on the outside of his right heel, and a florist whose wooden clogs announced her from halfway down the block. When the florist came in wearing sneakers one Saturday, my father looked genuinely startled, as if a person he knew had climbed in through a window.

I did not take over the business. I went away to study accounting, married a woman who taught swimming, and became competent at a number of things that would have bored my father senseless. He sold the shop when his fingers grew too stiff for stitching. For his retirement party we ordered a cake in the shape of a boot. The bakery made it bright blue, a color he had never once been asked to put on a shoe. He ate the heel standing up in the kitchen, still wearing the paper napkin my daughter had tucked into his collar.

After he died, my mother asked me to sort his tools. She wanted the cupboard for towels. I had imagined this as an afternoon of solemn decisions, but most of the cupboard contained dried tubes of glue and receipts from a supplier in Ohio. In a tobacco tin I found brass eyelets, three foreign coins, and a photograph of myself at twelve behind his counter. On the back he had written, in the block capitals he used on claim tickets, RADIO DEPARTMENT. I put the photograph in my pocket and threw away the glue. The tools went home with me in a grocery bag.

They stayed in the bag for almost four years. Then one wet evening my daughter came over with a loose strap on her sandal. She was twenty and had recently discovered that her parents owned various things she preferred not to buy. She had come for tape. Instead I got out the bag. We spread everything across the dining table: awls, pincers, a little hammer polished dark where his thumb had rested. I knew what each tool was called. To my considerable embarrassment, I had almost no idea what to do with any of them.

My daughter found a shoe repairer near the bus station. We took the sandal there the next morning. The man behind the counter examined the strap and asked whether she wanted the stitching to match. The original thread was yellow. He had brown, black, and a fierce pink left over from a dance costume. She chose pink and paid to have the sound strap restitched to match it. While we waited, I told him about my father’s shop. He asked what machine my father had used. I described its green paint and the noise it made. “That narrows it down to all of them,” he said.

I had expected the tools to make me sad. What bothered me instead was the loss of all those answers. For years I could have asked my father why he wet a piece of leather before stretching it, or what he listened for when he tapped a sole. I had been present for so much of the work that I mistook proximity for instruction. Yet I could remember, with useless precision, how he answered the telephone: “Yes, shoes,” as though settling an argument begun before the caller was born. My daughter still answers my calls that way when she is in a good mood.

The repairer bought most of the tools. I kept the hammer because it fit my hand, and because a hammer, unlike a curved needle, stood some chance of earning its keep in our house. A month later I used it to hang a shelf in the laundry room. The shelf sloped slightly toward the door. My wife set a marble on it to demonstrate the problem, and we watched the marble gather speed and drop neatly into a basket of clean socks. For a while we kept a marble beside the detergent so visitors could see the trick.

Last Sunday my daughter brought her little boy over for breakfast. He found the marble in a saucer of loose change. I carried him into the laundry room, cleared a space between the detergent and a box of clothespins, and showed him where to set it down. Each time it dropped he demanded another turn. From the kitchen my daughter called that our coffee was getting cold. I could hear her scraping the last of the good jam onto her toast. “Coming,” I called. The boy held out his hand. I fished the marble out of the socks and gave it back.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A carefully shaped family story whose quiet emotional weight grows through recurring details of repair, work, and passing time.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and gently wry, attentive to the small physical particulars that make people recognizable: a rooster clock, a heel striking pavement, orange peel on a radiator, a pink repair thread. Its grief is restrained rather than solemn. The narrator regrets having mistaken nearness to his father’s work for learning, but the story does not resolve that regret with a grand inheritance; instead, the tools pass through the narrator’s hands, a shelf slopes, and a marble becomes a game for a child. The reader is invited to notice how care and family memory can survive as habits, jokes, and shared time, even when the practical knowledge itself is lost.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds repair as both a trade and a way of attending to people: the clock that gives a couple more time over coffee, the father’s recognition of customers by their footsteps, and the narrator’s imperfect attempt to carry his work forward. It also selects intergenerational handoffs, ordinary domestic objects, and the gap between being present and truly learning. Its emotional center is not the tools alone, but the small moments of companionship they make possible.

## Evidence line
> I had been present for so much of the work that I mistook proximity for instruction.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The recurring repair objects, restrained grief, and warm comic turns give the sample a distinctive, coherent emotional and stylistic pattern.
